description:
Readiness for marriage is tested through responsibility and character. Wesam Saad begins with financial questions carried over from the previous session. He emphasises willingness to work, wise use of money and the ability to provide, rather than inherited wealth or a particular salary. Contentment matters alongside preparation for a distinct household. He then explains his view that shared finances should express the unity of marriage, while distinguishing temporary protection against serious financial wrongdoing from an ordinary pattern of independence. The discussion of doctrine returns to requirements and preferences: a shared gospel is essential, while other differences need careful consideration because they can still significantly affect married life.

Turning to a woman’s readiness, Saad uses Proverbs and Titus 2 to examine qualities that should already be developing before marriage. He discusses love for children, self-control, purity, care of the home, kindness and submission within his account of the responsibilities of wives. He distinguishes these responsibilities from differences in personal worth and repeatedly looks for direction of growth rather than perfection. Older women have an active role in helping younger women mature. The practical challenge is to cultivate these qualities now, so that the future household can serve others and pursue God’s purposes together rather than expecting marriage itself to transform unaddressed habits.

questions.question: What matters more than a particular salary when assessing financial readiness?
questions.answer: Saad looks for willingness to work, responsibility with money and the ability to provide for the household. Inherited money does not replace those habits, and a good income can still be wasted. He combines practical provision with contentment rather than setting a universal salary or wealth threshold.

questions.question: How does Saad explain shared bank accounts and the exception he discusses?
questions.answer: He presents shared finances from the beginning of marriage as an expression of becoming one household under the husband’s leadership. He separately describes temporary protection of funds when serious financial wrongdoing threatens provision, with accountability and restoration as the aim. He does not treat unresolved gambling before marriage as something a wedding will solve.

questions.question: What doctrinal agreement does the teacher treat as essential?
questions.answer: He says the prospective spouse must be in the Lord and hold the same gospel. A difference that changes the gospel is therefore not merely a preference. He also accepts the need for mature advice when someone may not recognise how a seemingly small doctrinal difference affects that central issue.

questions.question: Why can a doctrinal preference still matter greatly?
questions.answer: Saad asks listeners to consider the effect of a difference on church life, prayer, fellowship and the couple’s ability to live together faithfully. Calling something a preference does not mean it is insignificant. Its weight should be considered honestly with counsel rather than dismissed because it is not itself a gospel requirement.

questions.question: What responsibility does Titus 2 place on older women in this session?
questions.answer: Saad calls older women to take an active interest in younger women and help them grow in the qualities described. Household duties should not become a reason to neglect that ministry. He recognises that the passage directly addresses married younger women and then considers how developing qualities can be observed before marriage.

questions.question: What does looking for direction rather than perfection mean when assessing character?
questions.answer: The teacher seeks evidence that qualities such as self-control, purity and kindness are present and growing. He distinguishes a person who recognises weakness and wants to learn from someone who stubbornly refuses instruction. Marriage is not presented as a sudden cure for habits that are being ignored beforehand.

questions.question: How does the discussion distinguish love for children from the ability to have them?
questions.answer: Saad treats love for children and willingness to care for and teach them as matters of the heart. He explicitly recognises that God may not permit someone to have children. His argument therefore distinguishes physical inability from an unwillingness to welcome the responsibilities he describes.

questions.question: How are care of the home and kindness connected with serving others?
questions.answer: The home is described as a place of rest and hospitality that can support fellowship, teaching, prayer and evangelism. Saad warns that outward order alone is insufficient if it is accompanied by anger or resentment. He looks for patient, gracious care that reflects an inward disposition as well as completed tasks.

questions.question: How does the teacher explain submission without claiming unequal personal worth?
questions.answer: Saad distinguishes his understanding of authority within marriage from the equal value of men and women before God. He then treats a single woman’s response to parental authority as relevant preparation for the responsibilities he assigns to a wife. The emphasis is on learning the character he believes will carry into married life.
